headline_en: National Expatriates' Day observed in Lebanon
summary_en: The Bangladesh Embassy in Beirut marked National Expatriates' Day 2023 by closing its 'Special Service Week' (22 to 31 December 2023) on Tuesday 2 January 2024. For the first time the embassy honoured the top senders of remittance through legal channels from Lebanon in 2023; nine workers including two women were honoured. A public hearing was held before the ceremony. The article is based on a press release.

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Embassy in Beirut ran a 'Special Service Week' from 22 to 31 December 2023 for Bangladeshis in Lebanon, offering special consular and welfare services alongside its regular services; Ambassador Air Vice Marshal Javed Tanveer Khan opened it on 22 December.

The closing event of the Beirut embassy's Special Service Week was held at the Bangladesh Embassy premises in Beirut on Tuesday 2 January 2024 at 12 noon, marking National Expatriates' Day 2023; messages from the President, Prime Minister, Home Minister, Foreign Minister and Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister were read out.

For the first time the Bangladesh Embassy in Beirut honoured the highest senders of remittance through legal channels from Lebanon in 2023 with certificates, crests and gifts; 9 Bangladeshi migrant workers in Lebanon, including 2 women, received the honour.

As part of the Special Service Week, the Bangladesh Embassy in Beirut held a 'public hearing' (gonoshunani) from 10:30 am to 12 noon on 2 January 2024, attended by a large number of Bangladeshi women and men working in Lebanon.
30 December is declared National Expatriates' Day in Bangladesh; the ambassador to Lebanon said observing it each year would make embassy services for expatriates more dynamic.

headline_en: Higher education in South Korea: a realistic budget idea for Bangladeshi students
summary_en: A guide piece by the CEO of CHS Education Limited sets out what studying in South Korea costs a Bangladeshi student: average tuition by university type, monthly living costs, and the total first-year budget with and without tuition waivers. It names three national universities to look at, points to the Global Korea Scholarship 2027 undergraduate guideline, explains the D-2 and D-4 visas and warns that part-time work is not guaranteed. It ends with seven questions to ask before deciding.

facts.statement: According to the Korean government's Study in Korea portal, average annual tuition at 4-year universities in South Korea is about 68.2 lakh won (given as 6.2 lakh taka); at national and public universities about 42.7 lakh won (given as 3.93 lakh taka); at private universities about 76.3 lakh won (given as 7.2 lakh taka). Actual payable amounts may differ because of bank exchange rates and transaction charges.
facts.source_in_article: Study in Korea portal, cited by writer Nazmul Hasan Raju

facts.statement: According to official guidance, an international student's monthly cost in South Korea is roughly 7.5 lakh to 10 lakh won, covering housing, food, transport and daily expenses; the article gives the 12-month total as 8.24 lakh to 11 lakh taka.
facts.source_in_article: Korean government guidance, cited by the writer

facts.statement: In the article's budget section, annual tuition is put at about 3.98 lakh taka at a national or public university and about 7.12 lakh taka at a private university, and 12 months of living costs at 8.40 lakh to 11.20 lakh taka. These taka figures differ slightly from those given earlier in the same article (3.93 lakh and 7.2 lakh tuition; 8.24 to 11 lakh living).
facts.source_in_article: Writer Nazmul Hasan Raju, CEO of CHS Education Limited

facts.statement: Without a scholarship, the total initial annual cost of studying in South Korea is put at 12.38 lakh to 15.18 lakh taka at a public university and 15.52 lakh to 18.32 lakh taka at a private university. These are national-average planning figures, not any university's specific figures.
The South Korea study budget excludes airfare, application and admission fees, visa cost, document translation and attestation, initial set-up and an emergency fund.

Fees differ by programme in South Korea: engineering, natural science and laboratory-based subjects can cost more than humanities or social science, and housing and local costs in big cities like Seoul need to be checked separately.

Pusan National University (Busan) is suggested for students interested in engineering, science and business; its admission guideline lists tuition and dormitory costs by department, and it has some English-medium programmes.

Kyungpook National University (Daegu) is suggested for business, IT, engineering and science; its international admission page has information on tuition and scholarships based on TOPIK (Test of Proficiency in Korean), but conditions must be checked for each admission session.

Seoul National University (Seoul) is described as known for high-quality academic and research-based education; admission is competitive and tuition differs by department. Fees published in 2025 cannot be taken as confirmed fees for 2027.

Before applying to a South Korean university, check four things together: whether the programme really runs in English, whether Bangladeshi students can apply, the actual tuition for 2027, and how much you must pay yourself if you get a scholarship.

The official guideline for the Korean government's Global Korea Scholarship (GKS) 2027 at undergraduate level has already been published, and university-based application notices have also come out; students are advised to check eligibility, the university list, application method and deadlines now.
South Korean universities give their own scholarships; Kyungpook and Pusan offer tuition waivers based on TOPIK results, but these are conditional and not guaranteed for everyone.

Illustration of tuition waivers at a South Korean public university: with no scholarship the total initial annual cost is 12.38 to 15.18 lakh taka; with a 50 percent tuition waiver 10.39 to 13.19 lakh taka; with a 100 percent tuition waiver only living costs remain, 8.40 to 11.20 lakh taka. The waivers are for comparison, not a promise of any specific scholarship; fully funded GKS benefits and conditions must be checked separately.
For South Korea, the D-2 visa generally applies to degree programmes and the D-4 visa to language training.

According to the Korean embassy's instructions, a student visa application is made by filling in the e-form on the Korea Visa Portal and submitting it with the required papers; proof of financial capacity, bank statements and admission documents are needed. Applicants should check the latest rules before applying.
facts.source_in_article: Korean embassy instructions, cited by the writer

facts.statement: Part-time work for students in South Korea depends on visa conditions, permission, language ability and applicable rules; getting work is not certain, so possible earnings should not be treated as a substitute for the family's initial financing.

Without Korean language, daily life, job hunting and a long-term career in South Korea may need extra preparation; even where a degree can be done in English, local language skill widens future opportunities.

Seven questions to ask before deciding on South Korea: do my results and subject match the programme's eligibility; have I checked the programme language and IELTS/TOEFL or TOPIK conditions; do I have a written account of all costs including tuition, housing, food and insurance; have I verified scholarship eligibility, benefits, deadline and renewal conditions; can I prepare the visa's financial proof and documents; do I have money to continue studying even without part-time work; have I thought about career, language preparation and a back-up plan after the degree.

headline_en: Promise of well-paid jobs and marriage to suitable grooms: how they fell into traffickers' trap
summary_en: Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) rescued nine people at South Lombori Ghat, Teknaf Sadar union, Cox's Bazar, on the evening of Saturday 7 November 2026 as they were being gathered for trafficking to Malaysia by sea. Ten to fifteen members of the trafficking ring escaped by boat. The rescued said men were lured with good jobs and women with promises of marriage to suitable grooms in Malaysia.

facts.statement: BGB rescued 9 people at about 6:30 pm on Saturday 7 November 2026 in a raid at South Lombori Ghat (দক্ষিণ লম্বরীঘাট) in Teknaf Sadar union, Cox's Bazar, while they were being trafficked to Malaysia via the Teknaf sea coast; 10 to 15 members of the trafficking ring fled out to sea in a boat.

The nine rescued at Teknaf were Amir Hossain (45), Md. Jibon (19), Jannat Ara (17), Abdul Khalek (29), Foysal Karim (16), Ariful Islam (21), Nurul Islam (22), Ahmad Nabi (23) and Zahid Alam (18); some are residents of Rohingya refugee camps and the rest are from Cox's Bazar.

According to the rescued people's initial questioning, traffickers persuaded men to go to Malaysia by sea in wooden trawlers with the lure of good jobs, and promised women marriage to suitable grooms once taken to Malaysia.
facts.source_in_article: Lt Col Mohammad Tajul Islam Chowdhury, commander, Teknaf Battalion-2 BGB

facts.statement: The irregular sea route to Malaysia described: people are gathered at a boat landing (Lombori Ghat, Teknaf, Cox's Bazar) in the evening and sent by sea in wooden trawlers.
BGB said work was under way to establish the detailed identities of the nine rescued and efforts continued to catch the traffickers who fled.

headline_en: Family of West Bengal's Sahabuddin, who shared video of two Bangladeshis executed in Saudi Arabia, in anxiety
summary_en: After Saudi Arabia executed two Bangladeshis, Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Sweety Akter, over alleged immoral acts inside a mosque in Mecca, the family of Sheikh Sahabuddin, an Indian migrant mosque cleaner from Murshidabad, fears for him. He was arrested in 2023 for posting video of the incident on social media and is serving a prison sentence in Saudi Arabia. Indian migrant-support groups have contacted India's foreign ministry and embassy.

facts.statement: In mid-October 2026 the Saudi Interior Ministry announced the execution of two Bangladeshi nationals, Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Sweety Akter, under 'tazir' law, on the charge of engaging in immoral acts inside a mosque in Mecca; the article says this was three years after the incident.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter, citing Saudi Interior Ministry announcement

facts.statement: Sheikh Sahabuddin, an Indian migrant worker from Balarampur village, Murshidabad, West Bengal, who worked as a cleaner at the Mecca mosque, was arrested in 2023 on a charge of disrespectful conduct at the mosque; another young man present filmed the two Bangladeshis with Sahabuddin's mobile phone and Sahabuddin later spread the video on social media. A Saudi court sentenced him to imprisonment and he is now in a Saudi prison.
facts.source_in_article: Reporter, citing Indian media and the family

facts.statement: Saudi authorities treated posting the video of the incident inside the Mecca mosque on social media as a serious offence that damaged the dignity of a holy place; the poster was arrested quickly and jailed.

Sahabuddin's family says he is innocent and posted the video on a whim without understanding its gravity; organisations and social workers helping Indian migrant workers have contacted India's Ministry of External Affairs and the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia to get him freed and returned.

Related headlines embedded in the article state that Bangladesh sent a letter to Saudi Arabia seeking answers to 6 questions about the execution of the two, and that a father spoke to his daughter for the last time the day before the execution.

The Expatriates' Welfare Ministry named them as Sajal Chandra Das of Cumilla and Mohammad Abdur Rahim of Noakhali; they fainted from heat and smoke, have no serious injuries and are in the Saudi-German Hospital in Dammam. The article cites Al Jazeera on a series of attacks on Saudi airports.

headline_en: Government failed to act to protect its own citizens' lives: CPB
summary_en: The Communist Party of Bangladesh (CPB) held a protest rally in front of the National Press Club in Dhaka on Thursday 22 October 2026 over the execution of two Bangladeshis in Mecca, Saudi Arabia. Its leaders said the government failed to protect its citizens, noted that the Foreign Ministry said it knew nothing of the charges, trial or verdict, and demanded a list of Bangladeshis detained abroad, state-funded legal aid and regular prison visits.

facts.source_in_article: Abdullah Kafi Ratan, CPB General Secretary

facts.statement: At a rally in front of the National Press Club, Dhaka, at about 11:30 am on 22 October 2026, CPB demanded a full investigation of every expatriate death abroad, action to free Bangladeshis jailed abroad, and effective diplomatic initiative, legal aid and accountability to protect Bangladeshis working abroad.

CPB presidium member Ragib Ahsan Munna demanded that the government make a list of Bangladeshis detained or imprisoned abroad, give expatriates legal aid at state expense, and set up regular prison visits and contact with prisoners' families; he called for urgent diplomatic steps to free Bangladeshis jailed in Saudi Arabia and other countries.

headline_en: Two Bangladeshis executed in Saudi Arabia: embassy did not know
summary_en: A short item says the Bangladesh Embassy is angry at the execution of Bangladeshis Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter in Saudi Arabia, of which Saudi authorities did not inform it before or after; news came through the media on 14 October. They were detained in August 2023. The embassy has sent a diplomatic note asking for a copy of the verdict.

facts.statement: Saudi authorities did not inform the Bangladesh Embassy before or after executing Bangladeshis Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter; the news came through the media on 14 October (2026).

Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter were detained in Saudi Arabia in August 2023 on allegations relating to information technology and adultery, but a charge of violating the sanctity of a mosque in Mecca was brought.
The Bangladesh consulate said the list of detainees it received did not mention any punishment for the two, and that a death sentence on such charges is rare.
The Bangladesh Embassy sent a diplomatic note to Saudi authorities asking for a copy of the verdict in the case of the two executed Bangladeshis.

headline_en: Why barring three women from going abroad is not beyond legal authority: High Court
summary_en: On Tuesday 29 September 2026 a High Court bench issued a rule asking why stopping three adult women from travelling abroad should not be declared without lawful authority, and why authorities should not be directed to issue guidelines against blocking adult women's lawful travel for being unmarried or unaccompanied. The women were stopped at the airport despite valid passports, visas or entry permissions and tickets. The court ordered the police's Additional IGP to dispose of their complaint in seven days and immigration not to obstruct their next trip if papers are in order.

facts.statement: A High Court bench of Justice K M Kamrul Kader and Justice Fatema Anwar on 29 September 2026 issued a rule asking why the action of obstructing three women's travel abroad should not be declared beyond lawful authority, and why the authorities should not be directed to frame and issue guidelines not to obstruct adult women citizens' lawful foreign travel merely for being unmarried, travelling without a guardian or similar gender-based considerations.
facts.source_in_article: High Court order; lawyer Ishrat Hasan

facts.statement: Three adult women were stopped from leaving Bangladesh at the airport despite having valid passports, visas or entry permission and air tickets; immigration asked whether their families knew, told them to phone home (which they did), and said they were unmarried and travelling on their own. facts.statement: The three women filed a written complaint with the Additional Inspector General of Police on 30 August (2026) asking for an investigation into why they were stopped and action against those involved; getting no result, they filed a writ petition in the High Court.

The High Court directed the Additional Inspector General of Police to dispose of the three women's complaint within seven days and file a report, and directed the immigration authority not to obstruct the petitioners' next foreign trip if they have proper papers.

The petitioners' lawyer argued that stopping adult women from travelling for being unmarried or unaccompanied raises questions under Constitution articles 27 and 28 (equality and non-discrimination by sex), 31 and 32 (protection of law and personal liberty) and 36 (freedom of movement); the petitioners said whether an adult woman is unmarried or accompanied by parents or a guardian cannot be an independent legal basis to control a citizen's lawful travel abroad.

facts.statement: The columnists describe Bangladesh's current exchange-rate system as a loosely managed float within an undeclared band, in which the central bank is reported to set acceptable exchange-rate limits for commercial banks by informal verbal instruction; they warn that when banks cannot legally transact above a set rate, remittances easily shift back to hundi and a foreign-currency black market forms.

facts.statement: The columnist proposes a 'PIE' framework (Philanthropy, Investment, Expert Engagement) and a high-powered 'National Platform for Diaspora Engagement in National Development' working from the Prime Minister's Office, possibly headed by the Prime Minister, with a Project Implementation Unit; the Economic Relations Division (ERD) could implement it in the short term. Challenges named by the columnist: there is no reliable long-term online database of expatriates; many expatriates live in countries where they have no legal residence permit and so are unwilling to disclose personal information; and many expatriate associations abroad are influenced by Bangladesh's national politics.

headline_en: Family overwhelmed to get back missing migrant Amir Hossain after 30 years
summary_en: Amir Hossain of Dinara village, Naria, Shariatpur, went to Malaysia through a broker in 1996, lost contact with his family after three years and was missing for 27 years. Six months ago two Bangladeshis found him mentally unwell in a tin hut in a forest in Penang and posted video; his wife recognised him. After the Bangladesh mission verified his identity through the Naria UNO, a birth registration was issued and the mission gave a travel pass; he landed in Dhaka at 12:20 am after the night of Tuesday 21 April 2026 and was received by BRAC Migration Programme and family.

facts.statement: Amir Hossain of Dinara village, Chamta union, Naria upazila, Shariatpur, sold inherited farmland and went to Malaysia through a broker in 1996, worked there as a painter, kept in touch and sent money home every month for three years, then contact stopped and the family had no trace of him for 27 years.

Six months before his return, an expatriate named Dipu and expatriate journalist Bappi Kumar Das found Amir Hossain in a mentally unbalanced state in a small tin hut in a forest in Penang, Malaysia, rescued him and posted photos and video on social media; his family recognised him from the video and contacted the person who posted it, then spoke to him on video calls several times. (The son's quote spells the journalist's name 'Pappi Kumar Das'.)

How an undocumented, long-missing Bangladeshi was repatriated from Malaysia: Bangladesh mission officials in Malaysia sent his photo and the information he gave to the Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) of Naria for verification; the UNO verified it with the family; with upazila administration help Chamta Union Parishad issued a birth registration for him; that birth registration and family members' documents were sent to the Bangladesh mission in Malaysia, which then issued a travel pass and arranged his return.
Amir Hossain arrived in Dhaka from Malaysia at 12:20 am in the night following Tuesday 21 April 2026, about 30 years after leaving; the whole effort took about six months.

At the Dhaka airport, BRAC Migration Programme and family members received Amir Hossain with help from Civil Aviation Security (AVSEC) and the Probashi Kallyan (expatriates' welfare) Desk; he was then taken to his younger son Shahidul Islam's home in Keraniganj, Dhaka.
Naria UNO Abdul Qayyum said the upazila administration would stand by the returnee in any problem.

BRAC Associate Director (Migration and Youth Platform) Shariful Hasan said the case shows the uncertainty of migrant life, that nobody knows how many others are in such a crisis, and that a database of every expatriate is not impossible in this age of technology but necessary.

After Amir Hossain went missing, his wife raised six children with help from relatives and neighbours; the children could not study for lack of money and worked as labourers from childhood, according to son Babu Talukdar, who was six when his father left.

headline_en: I could not even see my son one last time
summary_en: First-person account by Akhlus Mia of Sunamganj, whose son Shayek Ahmad was one of 22 people who died of lack of water and food on 21 March 2026 in a small boat crossing the Mediterranean to Greece. The father had earlier lost 4.5 lakh taka to a broker for a Serbia trip that never happened, then paid broker Azizul Islam of Ichhgaon 4.5 lakh taka up front and 7.5 lakh more after Shayek reached Libya via Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Egypt. In Libya Shayek was held in a crowded room, starved and tortured for money.

facts.statement: On 21 March 2026, 22 people died from lack of water and food while crossing the Mediterranean in a small boat on the way to Greece; one was Shayek Ahmad of Sunamganj.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo introduction; father Akhlus Mia

facts.statement: Akhlus Mia of Sunamganj says that two years ago he sold some land and paid a broker 4.5 lakh taka to send his son Shayek to Serbia; the trip kept being postponed and never happened, the money was lost and could not be recovered from the broker.

For the Libya-to-Greece trip arranged through broker Azizul Islam of Ichhgaon (ইছগাঁও), the terms were 4.5 lakh taka up front and the remaining 7.5 lakh taka after reaching Libya, before being put on the 'game'; the father paid the first 4.5 lakh, then sold the household cows and land to send the further 7.5 lakh taka (12 lakh taka in all by these figures). The agreement was verbal.

Shayek left home with several others from his village about four months before the account and travelled first to Saudi Arabia, then Kuwait, then Egypt, to Libya; the promise was that he would be sent from Libya to Greece in a large wooden boat.

'Game' is the word used for going by sea from Libya to Greece in small wooden or plastic boats at the risk of one's life; the father says he knew of hundreds of young men dying in 'games', including two boys from his own area two years earlier.

Brokers said the migrants were in a 'camp' in Libya, but it was one room into which everyone was crammed, with too little food: a kind of hostage situation. Many had their phones taken; they were beaten for money and photos and videos of the beatings were sent to families so that money would be sent quickly. Shayek too was tortured for money, was not given food and was at times cut off from contact.

Shayek once cried on the phone asking his father to arrange his return from the Libya 'camp', saying he would not survive; the broker ignored the father, saying time was up and the 'game' could be any time.

Shayek missed one boat departure because he fell and hurt his leg running on the seashore. On 21 March he phoned to say there was a 'game' that day that he probably would not be on and that he would go on the 23 March one; in fact he was on the 21 March boat.
On 23 March the father could not reach Shayek and the broker did not answer the phone; the family learned of the death only on 28 March from people in the area.
The father, Akhlus Mia, had himself worked in Kuwait for 18 years and wanted his son to study and stay in Bangladesh; he says the son became obsessed after seeing local boys leave for Europe.

headline_en: Language study abroad: Probashi Kallyan Bank giving loans of 10 lakh taka without collateral
summary_en: Probashi Kallyan Bank has launched a 'loan for language learning and special skills for overseas employment' scheme giving up to 10 lakh taka without collateral for admission to language courses in countries including Japan, Korea, China and Germany. The loan covers tuition sent directly to the institution and living costs abroad. Conditions include age up to 40, an offer letter, a minimum language certificate, 11 percent annual interest and a term of up to three years; helpline 16238.

facts.statement: Probashi Kallyan Bank has launched the scheme 'Loan for language learning and acquiring special skills for the purpose of overseas employment' (বৈদেশিক কর্মসংস্থানের উদ্দেশ্যে ভাষা শিক্ষা ও বিশেষ দক্ষতা অর্জনের জন্য ঋণ), under which eligible applicants get up to 10 lakh taka as a loan without collateral for admission to language courses in countries including Japan, Korea, China and Germany.

The Probashi Kallyan Bank language-study loan can be used to send tuition fees directly to the educational institution concerned and to send money for accommodation and food costs while abroad; easy terms are highlighted especially for students going to Korea, Japan, China and Germany.

To get the Probashi Kallyan Bank language-study loan the applicant must be a local resident of the branch's area and not more than 40 years old, and must show an offer letter issued by an educational institution in the destination country and a language certificate of at least intermediate level (for example N5 for Japan, TOPIK Level 3 for South Korea).

Documents to submit with the Probashi Kallyan Bank language-study loan application: passport-size photo, copy of national identity card, educational certificates and the necessary papers relating to the guarantor.
The Probashi Kallyan Bank language-study loan carries annual interest of 11 percent and a maximum term of three years; other fees and charges are set by the bank's policy.
For details on the language-study loan, contact the nearest Probashi Kallyan Bank branch or the helpline number 16238; information is also on the bank's website (address not printed).

headline_en: Amid war, Bangladeshi expatriates in the Middle East spend Eid in fear
summary_en: With the war that began when the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February 2026 spreading to other Middle East countries, Bangladeshis in Qatar, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Oman describe an Eid-ul-Fitr under restrictions: movement limits, Eid prayers only inside mosques, police safety briefings and cancelled flights home. Several Bangladeshis have been killed in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, the UAE and Iraq. Bangladesh embassies advise expatriates not to post war-related content on social media; in Bahrain people are being arrested for doing so.

facts.statement: The article says more than 50 lakh Bangladeshis live in the war-affected countries of the Middle East, and that during the war several Bangladeshis have been killed in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, the Emirates and Iraq.

In Qatar the government continually sends warnings and emergency instructions by SMS to residents' mobile phones and tells people not to go outside when the situation worsens; police visit workplaces and have instructed staff how to move quickly to a safe place with customers if an alarm sounds.
facts.source_in_article: Kabir (pseudonym), accountant at a bank in Al-Shahaniya, Qatar, 7 years in the country

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi in Al-Shahaniya, Qatar, said bombs hit 10 to 15 km from his workplace, there were days with two or three attacks, and he had to stay indoors for 10 days in a row. Movement has been somewhat eased in Al-Shahaniya, but free movement remains stopped in areas such as Ain Khaled, Al Waab and Lusail City for fear of Iranian attack.
In Qatar, for security, Eid-ul-Fitr 2026 prayers have to be said inside mosques instead of in open fields, and free movement between most cities is stopped.

Aziz Ahmed (pseudonym) of Narsingdi, 9 years with a cleaning company in Al-Jahra, Kuwait, had a ticket home for 16 March 2026 but could not travel because airports and flights were temporarily shut after the war began.
Kuwait's administration announced that there would be no Eid congregation in the open or on large fields in 2026 and that everyone should pray in mosques.

Kuwait police called a meeting of expatriates and explained in Arabic and English what to do immediately and how to take shelter if a war warning or siren sounds; expatriates are told to follow the administration's instructions and warnings when commuting. The worker said he and colleagues also follow emergency instructions from the Bangladesh Embassy.

In Saudi Arabia there is fear in the eastern areas, especially those on the Gulf coast, and extra caution in Riyadh, while the situation is normal in the western cities of Mecca, Medina and Jeddah, where people are going to work and shopping for Eid. In Gulf countries, expatriates in areas with US bases are in the most frightening situation.
facts.source_in_article: Two Bangladeshi expatriates in Mecca and Jeddah; reporter

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi in Manama said an Iranian attack a few days earlier caused deaths in Bahrain and many now do not go out unless necessary.
A Bangladeshi in Manama said many people in Bahrain are being arrested for publishing anything war-related online.
A Bangladeshi in Manama said expatriates fear losing work, and that many Bangladeshi expatriates who have gone home to Bangladesh fear losing their jobs.
A Bangladeshi in Sohar, Oman, said he wanted to spend Eid in Bangladesh but could not return because of the war; the situation in his city is largely normal, though people fear an attack at any time.

Bangladesh embassies in various countries are advising expatriates to refrain from publishing war-related information or spreading news on social media. The Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh, in an urgent notice in the first week of March 2026, asked expatriates, in respect of Saudi local law, not to upload any related photo or video, or publish, share, like or comment on any such news on social media.
